summary:
Limpopo is a province of the Republic of South Africa and stands under the national legal framework. The province-specific material in the source inventory concerns the reach of customary law and traditional authority in the rural districts that formed part of the former Bantustans.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 May 2012 that the Traditional Courts Bill then before parliament would create a parallel customary-law justice system covering people living in the former Bantustan areas, with no provision allowing anyone to opt out of its jurisdiction. The same report states that rural LGBT people already face discrimination, violence and poor police cooperation, and that chiefs' courts punish lesbians in rural areas.

Mamba Online reported on 18 April 2012, in a piece by Melanie Judge, that the bill was under debate in provincial public hearings and would re-criminalise gay and lesbian conduct in former-Bantustan areas through a separate customary system. Lesbians were reported punished at chiefs' homesteads and tribal offices, and those able to do so were expected to leave rural areas. Traditional leaders were also reported to have opposed the Civil Union Act of 2006.

The most recent documented instance in this record dates from 2012; no later instance is documented.
tangentialFactors:
The exposure described here runs through a second, customary justice track rather than through the national courts, which is the mechanism that distinguishes Limpopo's rural former-Bantustan districts from the province's urban centres. The reported conduct of traditional leaders, including opposition to the Civil Union Act of 2006, indicates institutional hostility at the level of the authorities operating that track.

The 2012 reports describe a bill under debate, not an enacted instrument, and the record contains no account of its passage or of any later customary-law instrument applying to the province.
localsOnly: Rural residents of Limpopo's former-Bantustan districts were reported in 2012 to be subject to chiefs' courts with no mechanism to decline that jurisdiction, and to face poor police cooperation when seeking state protection. The reported practical response of those able to exercise it was to leave rural areas.
outOfScopeNotes:
The current status of the Traditional Courts Bill is unresolved in this record: whether it was enacted, amended or withdrawn after the 2012 reporting is not sourced here, and no later assessment of customary-court jurisdiction in Limpopo is documented.

No Limpopo-specific material is sourced on identity documents or gender markers, entry and border screening, facility or bathroom access, access to gender-affirming care, hate-crime enforcement, or partner recognition. Those layers sit with the national record.

The 2012 reports concern lesbians and gay and bisexual people; no Limpopo-specific account of violence or discrimination targeting transgender residents is documented in this inventory.
